Chapter 4. Choosing the Right Hill — The Importance of Direction Before Persistence.
So, let’s talk about something that’s easy to overlook—direction. You know, putting in effort is great, but what if all that hard work is heading in the wrong direction?
Picture this: you’re climbing a hill with everything you’ve got, sweat pouring, muscles burning... but it turns out, it’s not even the hill that leads to where you want to go. No matter how hard or how long you climb, if you’re on the wrong path, you’ll never reach the summit that really matters.
This idea isn’t just for mountaineers. It pops up everywhere—careers, businesses, relationships, even personal goals. There are so many opportunities out there, but not all of them are created equal. Some paths lead to real achievement, others to dead ends. The challenge? Choosing wisely before you go all in.
Imagine you’re standing at the bottom of a bunch of hills. Each one is a different pursuit. Some are tall and tough, others are short and easy. It’s tempting to go for the easy ones, right? But honestly, those rarely give you the views—or the rewards—you’re hoping for. The greatest achievements? They’re usually at the summit of the hardest climbs.
So, how do you choose? Well, it starts with a little honest self-assessment... and some research. Ask yourself the tough questions—what are your real strengths? Where’s the actual demand? What’s the long-term potential? Sometimes, you’ll have to walk away from something that looks good on the surface, but deep down, it just isn’t the right fit.
Here are a few practical ways to pick your “hill” with care:
First, look for places where your strengths match up with real opportunities—where you can make an impact or earn a genuine reward.
Then, check if the path has a clear dip—a tough stretch that, if you can push through, leads to something truly worthwhile.
Try to avoid crowded paths where everyone’s competing, but there’s not much reward for being the best.
And, watch out for paths that look super easy—they might just lead to mediocrity or a total dead end.
Once you’ve picked the right hill, that’s when it makes sense to dig in and persist. Knowing your struggle is actually worth it? That’s powerful motivation to push through the hard parts. But if you realize the hill isn’t worth it, there’s no shame in quitting early and saving your energy for something better.
This whole approach takes a mix of humility and ambition. Humility to admit when something’s not working, and ambition to search for the path with the most potential for growth and achievement.
So here’s the main takeaway: direction comes before effort. The people and organizations that succeed most? They pick their hills with care, and then they put everything they have into climbing them. They don’t waste energy on paths that lead nowhere—they focus where the rewards are greatest, and they’re not afraid to quit everything else.
